column2: The Niagara Frontier Transportation Authority is asking the federal Urban Mass Transportation Administration for a $269 million grant (80% of a $336.25 million total) to build a 6.4-mile Light Rail Rapid Transit line along Main Street in Buffalo, New York, connecting downtown's Memorial Auditorium to the State University of New York at Buffalo (SUNYAB) South Campus. Most of the line (5.2 miles) would run in subway, with a 1.2-mile at-grade section including a car-free pedestrian mall on Main Street between Tupper and Church Streets, 14 stations, and 47 electric light rail vehicles. The corridor passes through central Buffalo neighborhoods with disproportionately Black, low-income, elderly, and transit-dependent populations (nearly half Black in 1970; nearly 60% of families in the Ellicott sub-area under $6,000 income). The EIS compares the proposed line against a 'No Action' Improved Bus System benchmark, advanced bus systems, commuter rail, heavy rail transit, and multiple light rail configurations, and selected the Minimum LRRT as best overall despite higher capital cost. Main environmental effects include property takings (about 21 parcels plus additional land for one of three candidate service yards), construction traffic and noise disruption, modest air-quality improvements (~6% carbon monoxide reduction) offset by small increases in nitrogen and sulfur oxides from feeder buses, and long-term benefits of about 2,500 fewer autos entering the CBD daily in 1995 and $14.3 million in annual user savings. The project has been publicly discussed since 1969, drew community opposition to earlier elevated alignments (leading to a redesigned mostly-subway route), and won 'nearly all favorable' comment at the July 1974 hearing plus unanimous backing from New York's congressional delegation in 1976.

column2: The Niagara Frontier Transportation Authority (NFTA) is seeking a $269 million federal grant from the Urban Mass Transportation Administration toward a $336.25 million project to build a 6.4-mile Light Rail Rapid Transit line along Main Street from Buffalo's downtown Memorial Auditorium to the SUNY at Buffalo South Campus. About 5.2 miles would run in subway (3.5 miles bored through rock, 1.7 miles built by cut-and-cover — a trench dug from the surface and covered back over) and 1.2 miles at street level, with 14 stations (eight underground, six at-grade), 47 electric articulated light rail vehicles powered by overhead catenary wires, and Main Street between Tupper and Church Streets converted into a car-free pedestrian mall. Three sites near the southern end — the South, Ellicott, and Terminal yards — are candidates for the vehicle storage and maintenance facility. The state of New York would cover the 20% local share of $67.25 million.

column2: The line passes through central Buffalo neighborhoods along Main Street, from the downtown Central Business District up to the SUNYAB South Campus, in a metropolitan area that has been losing population since 1970. Corridor residents are disproportionately Black (nearly half of the corridor population in 1970, versus about 20% citywide), low-income (nearly 60% of families in the Ellicott sub-area and over 40% in Masten had incomes under $6,000 in 1969), older (about a quarter to a third elderly), and highly transit-dependent — 98% of the Ellicott and Masten population had no car in 1970, and unemployment there topped 35% in 1975. At least 30,000 people in the City of Buffalo were estimated to be handicapped in ways relevant to public transport. Acoustically sensitive institutions near the alignment include Sisters of Charity Hospital, St. Mary's School for the Deaf, St. Francis Hospital, Canisius College, St. Paul's Cathedral, Buffalo General Hospital, and Roswell Park Memorial Institute; only one four-unit residence would need to be acquired along the trunk line, but service-yard sites would displace warehouses and small businesses (fewer than 100 employees).

column2: The EIS evaluates seven categories of alternatives: keeping and expanding current bus service (the 'No Action' Improved Bus System benchmark), advanced bus systems with bus-only lanes and busways (including a rejected 7-mile Bus Subway), commuter rail on existing tracks (dismissed because no suitable right-of-way serves the corridor and CBD), Heavy Rail Transit (a fully grade-separated system in 11-mile and 6.6-mile versions), Light Rail Transit in nine configurations, Light Rail Rapid Transit — light rail running mostly in its own right-of-way — in five configurations with possible Amherst, Tonawanda, and North Tonawanda extensions, and options for elevated structures. A two-stage screening (first economic, then service and social/environmental factors) ranked the Minimum LRRT System first, and it was selected as best overall despite higher capital cost ($246 million versus $5.8 million for Improved Bus). Three elevation variants were also compared: an all at-grade line was rejected because it would reduce Main Street to four lanes; a fully elevated line was rejected due to citizen rejection and cost; and a fully underground alternative was technically feasible but $33 million (13%) more expensive. Three candidate service-yard sites — South, Ellicott, and Terminal — remain under consideration, with total costs of about $9.07 million, $8.91 million, and $7.16 million respectively (1974 dollars).

column2: Long-term benefits would include better downtown access (especially for the elderly, people with disabilities, and people without cars), regional economic stimulus, a more pleasant pedestrian environment on the Main Street mall, and about 2,500 fewer autos entering the CBD daily in 1995 (a 15% reduction from existing counts), yielding $14.3 million in direct annual user savings and over $4 million in travel-time savings. Long-term harms include taking about 21 parcels (12 privately owned) along Main Street and razing 8 buildings; the service yard chosen would add further takings — the South Yard would take 2.1 acres of public and 7.7 acres of private land and raze 22 structures, while the Terminal Yard would take 8.3 acres of public land (including the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western Railroad depot) and 2.6 acres of private land. Energy analysis projects direct fuel savings of about 4.7% versus the Improved Bus benchmark in 1995 and net savings of about 2%, because autos would still account for nearly 90% of corridor passenger-miles. Air quality effects include reductions in carbon monoxide (~6.3%), hydrocarbons (~4.1%), and particulates (~4.4%) but small increases in nitrogen oxides (~5.3%) and sulfur oxides (~1.3%) from added feeder buses. Construction would generate about 910,000 cubic yards of spoil to be placed at NFTA-owned sites at Greater Buffalo International Airport or the Port of Buffalo, raising each site's surface about 6 feet, along with temporary traffic congestion, dust, noise, and vibration especially at cut-and-cover and at-grade sections. Operational noise on the at-grade mall section is expected to reach 70–75 dBA pass-by, meeting the 80 dBA American Public Transit Association Category 3 limit, with floating slab construction and resilient rail mounting used near sensitive receivers such as St. Paul's Cathedral, Marine Midland Tower, and the WKBW-TV studio. The New York State Historic Preservation Officer confirmed in a May 4, 1977 letter that the project will have no effect on National Register properties. The operating deficit is projected at $3.4 million annually in 1995, and assessed property values along the corridor could rise up to about 20% by 1995.

column2: The project has been under public discussion since 1969, with public hearings held in Buffalo in April 1972 and July 1974. Community opposition to earlier alignments and to long stretches of elevated ('aerial') structure forced route revisions after the 1972 hearings, and citizen rejection of aerial construction along Main Street was cited as a reason for dropping a fully elevated Light Rail Vehicle option. The July 1974 hearing on the revised 11-mile Heavy Rail Transit plan drew 'nearly all comment was favorable,' and the August 1976 hearing on the capital grant application also drew favorable citizen response. Local support was organized through the Joint Executive Committee for Rapid Transit — combining the Mass Transit Advisory Committee, the Area Committee for Transit, and the No Overhead Transit organization — and a 50-member Committee for Federal Action of business, civic, labor, and community leaders appointed in 1975; in February 1976 New York's entire congressional delegation united to press for federal approval. NFTA's Community Participation Program included 18 community forums and public hearings (about 2,120 attendees), 58 workshops, and 184 citizen/professional group meetings. The draft EIS was scheduled to be circulated beginning June 3, 1977 with a 45-day comment period (extendable by 15 days) and another public hearing set for July 14, 1977 in Buffalo; distribution includes citizens' groups such as the Sierra Club Niagara Group, Hamlin Park Community Association, and Erie County League of Women Voters. The Buffalo Landmark and Preservation Board reviewed the sites and found no problems with the project.
